result.summary: Do not close the design gate: recursive cleanup can still break a shelf’s resolution chain and destroy its originals on the second sweep.

findings.title: Protect intermediate links from recursive ancestor deletion
findings.body: X18 checks deletion targets against shelf anchors, but not against intermediate links’ locations. Consider `<state>/quarantine` → `<state>/cache/link` → `<core>/logs/recovery`, holding an original. Step 2 permits recursive deletion of `cache`: it overlaps neither the lexical shelf nor its resolved target. That deletes the intermediate link. The first sweep preserves `logs` using its cached anchors; the second sweep reconstructs anchors through the now-dangling shelf, no longer protects `logs`, and deletes the original. An in-memory model of the prescribed checks reproduced this sequence. X20’s explicit symlink-entry guard does not cover recursive deletion of the link’s parent. This affects direct disposer calls and aliases introduced after the gate, both explicitly supported scenarios.
findings.recommendation: Include every intermediate link’s location in the protected deletion surface. Require all recursive deleters to preserve directories containing those links. Add a regression with this two-hop alias across both disposer calls and a retry, asserting that the intermediate link and original bytes survive.

next_steps: Extend the resolution-chain guard to recursive ancestor deletions and rerun the design review.
